title: Connecting to APRS-IS & Radio
subtitle: Bring live APRS data in from the internet, a radio, or both — and confirm packets are actually flowing.
in_this_chapter: APRS-IS vs. RF, and why you can run both
The Connections tab: adding and editing ports
Setting up an APRS-IS port (server, passcode, filter)
Setting up a radio port (serial TNC, network TNC, AGWPE)
The Managed Modem tab for sound-card interfaces
The Ports tab and status badges
Confirming data is flowing with the Raw Packet Monitor

blocks.h1: What This Is / What It Is For

blocks.p: __APRS-IS__ is the worldwide internet network that carries APRS traffic, and __RF__ is what your radio hears off the air through a TNC or sound-card modem. This chapter is about getting live data flowing into APRS Command from either one — or both at once. Everything here lives on three tabs inside the Settings window: **Connections**, **Managed Modem**, and **Ports**.

Open all three from the menu bar with **Settings**. It opens the Settings window, and the tabs run along the top. **Connections** is where you define each way in and out. **Managed Modem** is a shortcut for people using a USB sound-card interface who want APRS Command to run the modem software for them. **Ports** is the read-only status board that tells you whether anything is actually arriving.

callout.label: Receive first, transmit off
callout.text: APRS Command listens by default and does not transmit until you deliberately turn transmit on. The title bar shows a **TX Disabled** badge whenever transmit is off. Nothing on the Connections or Managed Modem tab starts sending on its own — you can wire up APRS-IS and a radio and still be entirely receive-only.

blocks.h2: APRS-IS vs. RF — which do I want?

blocks.p: You do not have to choose just one. The note at the top of the Connections tab even says so: "Run more than one at once (for example a radio port and APRS-IS together)." Here is the short version of what each gives you.

rows: A connection to an internet APRS server
Packets your radio hears off the air
A TNC, or a sound-card modem
The whole network (you filter it down)
Only stations in radio range of you
Yes — leave the Transmit box unchecked

blocks.p: Open **Settings** and pick the **Connections** tab. The left side is your list of ports; the right side is the editor for whichever port is selected. A __port__ here just means one way APRS Command talks to the outside world — one APRS-IS server, or one radio interface.

steps: Below the list, pick a type from the dropdown: **APRS-IS**, **Network TNC (KISS-TCP)**, **AGWPE (TCP)**, **Serial KISS (hardware TNC)**, or **Managed local modem (sound card)**.
Click **Add**. A new port appears in the list, selected, with the editor showing its fields.
Fill in the fields on the right (covered below for each type).
Click **Save** at the bottom. The status line confirms, for example, `Saved 2 port(s).` Use **Revert** to throw away unsaved edits and reload the last saved list.

callout.label: New ports start disabled
callout.text: A freshly added port has **Enabled** unchecked, **Receive** checked, and **Transmit** unchecked. It will not do anything until you check **Enabled** and Save. This is deliberate — you build the port fully before it goes live.

blocks.h2: The three checkboxes on every port

blocks.p: Every port, whatever its type, has the same three checkboxes near the top of the editor:

bullets: **Enabled** — turns the whole port on or off. Off means APRS Command ignores it entirely.
**Receive** — lets packets come in from this port. Leave this on for normal listening.
**Transmit** — lets this port send. This stays off until you choose to turn it on. A radio or APRS-IS port with Transmit unchecked is receive-only, no matter what else is set.

callout.label: Transmit is a deliberate choice
callout.text: Checking **Transmit** on a port is the operator action that allows sending on that port. Even then, the app-wide transmit safety still applies — the title bar keeps showing **TX Disabled** until transmit is actually enabled, and Exercise Mode (Tools menu) blocks all transmit regardless. If you only want to watch traffic, leave Transmit unchecked everywhere.

blocks.p: Add a port of type **APRS-IS** and fill in the editor. The fields are:

bullets: **Server** — the APRS-IS server to connect to, for example `rotate.aprs2.net`.
**Port** — the server's TCP port number (the common APRS-IS filter port is `14580`).
**Passcode** — your APRS-IS passcode, a number worked out from your callsign. Enter `-1` for receive-only operation. A real passcode is only needed to transmit beacons and messages.

**Filter (optional)** — leave blank to use the automatic geographic filter from your Station Setup. To override it, enter a custom filter such as `m/100` or `r/41.97/-88.45/200`. The number is always in kilometers, regardless of your unit preference.
**Failover servers (optional)** — one `host:port` per line. If the primary server is unreachable for three or more minutes, APRS Command tries these in order.

callout.label: Receive-only APRS-IS
callout.text: Set **Passcode** to `-1` and you have a fully working receive-only feed — no callsign transmission, no risk of sending anything. This is the safest way to watch the network while you learn the app.

blocks.screenshot: The Connections tab with an APRS-IS port selected, showing the Server, Port, Passcode, Filter, and Failover servers fields, and the passcode set to -1.

blocks.p: "RF" means packets coming from your radio through a modem or TNC. APRS Command offers three ways to connect to one, plus the Managed Modem shortcut covered in the next section. Pick the type that matches your hardware.

rows: A hardware TNC on a USB/serial cable
A software modem already running that speaks KISS over TCP
An AGWPE / AGW host-mode packet engine

blocks.p: For **Serial KISS**, the **Serial port** field is a dropdown of ports found on this machine, but you can also type one in — the placeholder shows the format (`/dev/tty.usbserial` on Mac/Linux or `COM3` on Windows). Set **Baud** to match your TNC.
For **Network TNC (KISS-TCP)** and **AGWPE (TCP)**, enter the **Host** and **Port** where that software is listening. For a modem on the same computer, the host is usually `127.0.0.1`.

callout.label: Receiving over RF needs no transmit
callout.text: A radio port with **Enabled** and **Receive** checked will decode everything your radio hears, with **Transmit** left off. You get the full local picture on the map without ever keying the radio.

blocks.p: If your radio connects through a USB sound-card interface — a __DigiRig__, __SignaLink__, or similar — the **Managed Modem** tab lets APRS Command launch and manage a local __Direwolf__ modem process for you, instead of you running it by hand. Open **Settings** and pick the **Managed Modem** tab.

steps: Check that Direwolf is found. The tab shows a line reporting whether it located Direwolf. If it is installed via Homebrew or apt, leave the **Direwolf path** blank to use the system PATH; otherwise type the full path to the executable.
Pick **Audio input (from radio)** and **Audio output (to radio)** from the device dropdowns. Click the refresh button (↻) if a device you just plugged in is missing.

Under **PTT (Push to Talk)**, choose a **PTT method**: **None**, **Rts**, **Dtr**, or **GpioPin**. For Rts/Dtr a **PTT serial port** picker appears; for GpioPin a **GPIO pin (BCM number)** field appears (Raspberry Pi only).
Leave **Enable RF transmit** unchecked unless you intend to transmit (see the warning below).
Under **Advanced**, the **KISS TCP port** defaults to `8001` — change it only if something else is using that port.

callout.label: Enable RF transmit is the transmit switch here
callout.text: **Enable RF transmit** on this tab is what allows the managed modem to key your radio. Leave it unchecked to run the sound-card modem purely as a receiver. Even when it is checked, the app-wide transmit safety still applies and Exercise Mode will block transmit.

blocks.p: Once a managed modem is enabled and saved, it also shows up as a port on the **Ports** status board, so you can confirm it connected and is decoding.
There are three places to check that your connections are actually working: the title-bar badges, the **Ports** tab, and the **Raw Packet Monitor**.
Look at the top of the main window. The **APRS-IS** badge reports the state of your internet connection, and the **TX** badge reports your transmit state.

rows: Not connected to an APRS-IS server
Lost the server, retrying (failover may kick in)
Connection faulted — check the server and passcode
Transmit is off (the normal, safe state)

callout.label: The APRS-IS badge is only about the internet feed
callout.text: A radio (RF) port does not change the APRS-IS badge. If you are running RF only, the badge can read `APRS-IS Offline` while your radio port is happily receiving. Use the Ports tab to check RF.

blocks.p: Open **Settings** and pick the **Ports** tab. It lists every port with its **Type**, **State** (`Connected`, `Connecting`, `Disconnected`, `Reconnecting`, `Faulted`, or `Disabled`), **RX** and **TX** flags, a **Packets** count shown as received / transmitted, the **Last packet** time, and any **Last error**. The summary line at the top reads like `2/3 enabled, 1 connected, 148 RX, 0 TX`. If the received count is climbing, that port is working.

For the most direct proof, open **View → Raw Packets**. This window is described in the app as "Every packet received on all active ports, in arrival order. If packets appear here, the port is receiving." Watch the list — if lines are scrolling in, data is flowing. **Save Log** writes the feed to a file you can reopen later in the Replay window.

blocks.screenshot: The Raw Packet Monitor window with recent packets scrolling in, one line per received packet, and the Save Log button.

bullets: **Nothing shows up on the map after adding a port.** Open the **Ports** tab and check the port's **State**. If it says `Disabled`, go back to **Connections**, check **Enabled** on that port, and Save.

**APRS-IS badge stays `APRS-IS Offline`.** Confirm the port is enabled, the **Server** name is spelled correctly (for example `rotate.aprs2.net`), and the **Port** number is right. The badge only tracks APRS-IS, not RF.

**APRS-IS badge shows `APRS-IS Error`.** The server rejected or dropped the connection. Recheck the server, port, and passcode; a wrong passcode for your callsign is a common cause. Add a failover server if the primary is flaky.

**Connected to APRS-IS but flooded or barely any packets.** The **Filter** is too wide or too narrow. Leave it blank to use your Station Setup radius, or set something like `m/100`. Remember the filter number is in kilometers.

**Serial TNC port will not connect.** Verify the **Serial port** name matches your adapter (`COM3` on Windows, `/dev/tty.usbserial…` on Mac/Linux) and that **Baud** matches the TNC. Close any other program using that port.

**Managed modem does not start.** Check the Direwolf-found line on the **Managed Modem** tab. If Direwolf is in a custom location, type its full path; otherwise confirm it is installed and on your PATH. Make sure the **KISS TCP port** (default `8001`) is not already taken.

**Receiving fine but I want to be sure I am not transmitting.** Confirm the title bar reads **TX Disabled**, leave **Transmit** unchecked on every port and **Enable RF transmit** unchecked on Managed Modem, or turn on Exercise Mode from the **Tools** menu to inhibit all transmit.

**No packets in the Raw Packet Monitor.** No active port is receiving. Enable at least one port on **Connections**, confirm its **State** is `Connected` on the **Ports** tab, and check the antenna or audio path for RF ports.
